canberra.title: The rate that stops the nation: RBA saddles households with highest cash rate since 2008
canberra.snippet: The official interest rate is at its highest in 18 years, after the Reserve Bank raised the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 p...
canberra.content:
Jim Chalmers says the war in Iran has been devastating for the Australian economy. Photo: Jim Chalmers.

The official interest rate is at its highest in 18 years, after the Reserve Bank raised the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent.

Six board members voted to increase the rate, while three voted to leave it unchanged at 4.6 per cent.

The central bank’s cash rate has now reached its highest level since 2008.

“Inflation remains elevated and recent data indicate that it is broadly based. The inflation outlook has also been revised materially higher in the updated staff forecasts,” the RBA said in a statement released an hour before the Melbourne Cup began.

“This partly reflects higher fuel and other commodity prices affected by the conflict in the Middle East. But domestic capacity pressures are also judged to have been a little tighter than earlier thought.

“AI-related investment is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, and inflation in many goods and services remains high.”

It will be a hard blow to mortgage holders, small businesses and all Australians struggling with cost-of-living pressures.

Inflation rose to 4.3 per cent in the year to September.

Some banks have already announced they are passing the interest rate rise on to customers.

The RBA board said it was aware that inflation has been too high for too long.

“Given the revised inflation outlook and the continuing upside risks, the board judged that a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support the return of inflation to target,” it said.

“The board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target.”

Treasurer Jim Chalmers acknowledged that the RBA’s decision will be a tough pill for many Australians to swallow.

He noted that “people are under substantial pressure already” and increased borrowing costs will make it even harder for many.

The Treasurer again pointed to the Middle East conflict as having a major impact on the Australian economy, but denied the Federal Budget was a major contributing factor.

“Today’s decision was widely expected, but that doesn’t make it any easier for Australian families and businesses to absorb,” he said.

“It will be difficult news for many Australians who are already paying a hefty price for circumstances outside of their control … The war’s in its ninth month and its re-escalation is putting sustained upward pressure on inflation.

“It’s weighing on growth, and its end can’t come soon enough for the global economy or for Australians facing cost of living pressures.

“Our budgets are not what’s putting upward pressure on inflation. But we can play a helpful role, and that’s what we intend to do.”

When asked during a media conference following the RBA’s announcement whether he would consider stepping aside as Treasurer, he simply replied, “No”.

RBA Governor Michele Bullock also addressed the media, in a separate appearance, and acknowledged that the news was not what many Australians wanted to hear.

“But it is what’s needed to get inflation down … some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track,” she said.

“I understand that today’s decision is going to be difficult for Australians with mortgages, many of whom are already managing large repayments.

“But households with mortgages are not the only Australians doing it tough.

“Every household is dealing with higher prices for groceries, electricity, insurance and other essentials.

“High inflation is particularly painful for Australians on lower incomes, including people who rent and have little or no savings to fall back on.”

Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson laid the blame for rising interest rates squarely at the feet of Labor and the Federal Government’s use of taxpayers’ money.

“The Reserve Bank has been forced to raise interest rates on Australian families and small businesses for the 17th time under the Albanese Labor government because the taxaholic Treasurer still can’t kick his spending addiction,” he said.

“The only sure bet on Melbourne Cup Day was that Australian families would be forced to make tough choices because the Treasurer won’t kick his spending addiction.

“The RBA has now warned that because of the Treasurer’s spending addiction, rates are going to be high and stay there.

“Today’s rise adds around $150 a month to the average new mortgage. That family is now paying about $32,000 a year more in interest than when Labor was elected.

“That’s $2,700 a month ripped out of the family budget.”

canberra.title: Monaro Highway flyover ready to make journey south safer and smoother
canberra.snippet: A key component of the $260.5 million Monaro Highway Upgrade Program will open to traffic on Wednesday (4 November), making the drive to ...
canberra.content:
The Monaro Highway flyover will eliminate a traffic light stop on the southbound journey. Photo: iCBR.

A key component of the $260.5 million Monaro Highway Upgrade Program will open to traffic on Wednesday (4 November), making the drive to Canberra’s southern suburbs easier and safer for the 30,000 vehicles a day that use the vital transport corridor.

The new southbound Monaro Highway flyover at the Lanyon Drive Interchange should reduce delays for commuters, freight operators and visitors travelling between Canberra, Queanbeyan and southern NSW.

The 196-metre-long flyover will allow southbound through-traffic to bypass the traffic lights at the Lanyon Drive intersection, while those travelling to Queanbeyan and Jerrabomberra will continue to use the existing roadway to turn left at Lanyon Drive.

Southbound cyclists will temporarily remain on the existing southbound roadway and will be able to continue south by travelling through the existing traffic lights at the Lanyon Drive/Monaro Highway intersection. But they are expected to be able to travel over the bridge early next year.

A feature of the flyover is the Indigenous artwork, developed in consultation with Ngunnawal elders and community representatives, incorporated into Corten steel panels across the flyover, reflecting Ngunnawal stories and connection to the Monaro corridor.

Standing on the fresh tarmac, ACT City and Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne said the flyover would have wide-ranging benefits not just for ACT road users.

Ms Cheyne said people travelling from both the Cooma or Queanbeyan sides would benefit from the changed traffic arrangements.

She said the southbound journey would now be smooth and uninterrupted, with no waiting at traffic lights.

“If you are turning, obviously, into Queanbeyan and Jerrabomberra, you will still be going through those traffic lights, but for all of our Lanyon Valley residents and those in the south of Tuggeranong, heading south is going to be smoother.

“It’ll be a more reliable journey. It’ll be more efficient,” she said.

Member for Bean David Smith, Wodens project director Brad Maiden and City and Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Monaro Highway flyover. Photo: iCBR.

Monaro Highway flyover. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Monaro Highway flyover. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Monaro Highway flyover. Photo: iCBR

Ms Cheyne acknowledged that motorists had endured some pain over the past few years, but the traffic management had been well handled.

The flyover opening would allow the contractor, Wodens, to switch to the northbound side and complete works on Dog Trap Creek Bridge so it could open before Christmas.

The remaining elements of the initial interchange works should be completed in mid-2027.

Ms Cheyne did not expect new bottlenecks to develop further south.

Given the multiple projects underway across the ACT, the road network was handling the traffic demands well.

“We’ve had a really close look at how all of the traffic movements are responding to a lot of projects being underway at once, and overall, the network is handling it well, but this will make it handle it even better because we will have that smoother, more reliable journey for Canberrans heading south,” she said.

Federal environmental approvals for the balance of the Lanyon Drive Interchange have recently been received.

Heritage and geotechnical investigations as well as final designs for the remaining interchange works are now underway.

Construction of these remaining works, including the extension of David Warren Road, the new southbound off-ramp to Lanyon Drive, and the removal of the traffic signals at the Alexander Maconochie Centre, is expected to commence in 2028.

Planning is also underway for future upgrades along the Monaro Highway to support long-term transport needs, improve connectivity and enhance access for surrounding communities.

The Monaro Highway Upgrade Program is jointly funded by the Australian and ACT governments.

canberra.title: Inadequate prison supervision, weekend court gaps contributed to detainee’s death: coroner
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article discusses self-harm and death by suicide. An ACT coroner has highlighted mental health gaps across Canberra...
canberra.content:
Justin James Cordy died by suicide at Alexander Maconochie Centre (AMC) in 2023. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article discusses self-harm and death by suicide.

An ACT coroner has highlighted mental health gaps across Canberra’s justice system, but determined inadequate supervision behind bars ultimately contributed to an AMC prisoner’s death.

Justin James Cordy died on 26 February 2023 while he was a detainee at the Alexander Maconochie Centre (AMC). The 34-year-old took his own life two days after being arrested by ACT Policing officers. He had been released from prison just five days prior.

Coroner Lucinda Wilson’s findings outlined that the “much loved father, husband, son, brother and friend” also received poor treatment while he was in police custody, but this did not contribute to his death.

“In the AMC, he was given access to the implements he needed to complete suicide in his cell and was not adequately observed,” she determined.

“Had he been adequately observed, his preparations for suicide may have been identified, which should have led to intervention.”

This access was both to objects in a shared area and in his AMC ‘welcome pack’.

The exact time of Mr Cordy’s death was not known, as he was last seen alive at 11.40 am. This is despite the 34-year-old being on hourly observations while in custody.

CCTV showed a corrections officer looking through Mr Cordy’s cell door at 11.40 am, but not opening it, and no further checks were visible until 1.03 pm.

It was determined he died between then and 1 pm, when he was found in his cell.

Ms Wilson recommended changes to cell inspections, including requiring officers to enter cells for visual checks and spot-checking objects in shared areas.

Coroner Wilson stated police officers knew of Mr Cordy’s poor mental condition upon his arrest, as he told them “I’m going to kill myself” and “I’ve already cut myself” while holding a large knife to his wrist.

Other officers knew about his previous threats to harm himself, but these were not passed on to the arresting officers.

An ambulance was called upon Mr Cordy’s arrest, as he had run from police following a car crash, but the fact he’d self-harmed before his arrest was not explained to paramedics.

“I find that the attending officers at Justin’s arrest did not meet their obligations under the AFP Custody Guideline by virtue of calling the paramedic. That action was insufficient, especially given the lack of briefing to the paramedic, to meet their obligations under the guideline,” Ms Wilson determined.

“Even if, which I reject, Justin had cut his wrists four times whilst running from police, it remains their duty to care for the wellbeing of detainees. That duty remains whether the detainee has self-harmed in the seconds before arrest, or in the minutes before arrest.

“In either scenario, the police failed according to their own standards.”

Ms Wilson determined there wasn’t any evidence to suggest Mr Cordy would not have died if the officer’s considerations had been different.

She recommended further written guidance and training for police officers on assessing a detainee’s physical and mental health, communicating any concerns, and ensuring appropriate medical assessments were secured.

Ms Wilson raised concerns about a lack of resourcing for Canberra’s Saturday bail court list, which reduced the ability of that court to “adequately consider whether defendants before it should receive immediate mental health care and treatment”.

Issues raised included that the Mental Health Court Assessment and Liaison Service (MHCALS) doesn’t operate on Saturdays, and junior lawyers who appeared on the weekend “did so with limited training and no support”.

“The obligations on them were too high such that those appearing in the Saturday bail court do not receive the same level of service, or representation, as those who appear in the weekday bail courts,” Ms Wilson stated.

“This is not a reflection of the abilities of those individual lawyers, but of the system within which they were expected to work.

“Those defendants who have the misfortune to appear in the Saturday bail court cannot have their mental health considered in the same way as those who appear before the bail court on a weekday.

“This impacts the administration of justice.”

Ms Wilson found no “material difference” between the number of defendants who appeared before a weekday bail court and those who appeared on a Saturday listing.

She recommended better resourcing for the Saturday bail court, including more support and training for lawyers, and the availability of the MHCALS on weekends and public holidays.

Ms Wilson concluded by saying she hoped the recommendations would prevent further tragedy.

“It is my express wish that the failures in Justin’s supervision which contributed to his death will not occur again, and no other family will have to suffer the anguish experienced by Justin’s family from losing him too soon,” she said.

If you need help, or someone you know does, you can contact:

Lifeline’s 24-hour crisis support line – 13 11 14
Suicide Call Back Service – 1300 659 467
Kids Helpline – 1800 551 800 or kidshelpline.com.au
MensLine Australia – 1300 789 978.

canberra.title: Courtney Act as a junk sculpture at the National Portrait Gallery
canberra.snippet: Courtney Act, the renowned drag queen and stage name and alter ego of Shane Jenek, has been commemorated with a commissioned larger-than-...
canberra.content:
3 November 2026

Join the conversation

5

Paul Yore, In between, 2026, shells, crockery, glass, plastic, beads, buttons, sequins, glitter, found objects, fabric, trim, wood, adhesive, fixtures, synthetic polymer, enamel on board, overall: 178 cm x 125 cm. Photo: NPG.

Courtney Act, the renowned drag queen and stage name and alter ego of Shane Jenek, has been commemorated with a commissioned larger-than-life junk sculpture portrait by Paul Yore at the National Portrait Gallery.

Australia has a vibrant drag culture that goes back decades, from Les Girls and the iconic film The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert, to the more recent global stage of Drag Race Down Under.

Of Australian drag queen performers, Courtney Act is undoubtedly the most prominent, with a career spanning more than two decades and attracting a national and international audience.

Other Australian drag queens have tended to attract a more localised audience, such as Melbourne’s unforgettable Art Simone, Adelaide’s Kween Kong, Jojo Zaho, a First Nations queen from Newcastle, and the incredibly talented filmmaker and drag queen Lazy Susan.

A challenge for an artist commissioned to execute a portrait of a drag queen is what to show and what to highlight.

Is it simply the glitter of the façade to depict, or something more nuanced that shows the intellect behind the mask?

The problem was already beautifully spelt out in 1969 in John Brack’s great painting of Barry Humphries as the character Mrs Everage, in the Art Gallery of New South Wales collection and occasionally exhibited at the National Portrait Gallery in Canberra.

Brack carefully recorded Humphries’ famous fictional alter-ego, Dame Edna Everage, but on closer inspection, behind the pink glasses and mask appear the keen, watchful features of Humphries, and one quickly becomes aware that the outrageous clothes and oversized gloves hide a brilliant, alert intellect.

Visual artist Paul Yore at a preview of his exhibition ‘It’s All Wrong But It’s Alright’, on display at Hobart’s Black Temple Gallery (a deconsecrated colonial church) during the Dark Mofo festival in June. Photo: NPG.

Paul Yore is a young Gippsland-based artist who has built a reputation for working with banners, tapestries, quilted hangings and mixed media installations that engage with political, religious and LGBT themes. Critics have used terms like “kitsch queerness” and “bad taste aesthetic” to describe his art practice. He sometimes shocks, but always intrigues the viewer.

Yore was in awe of his subject. He is quoted as saying, “In the constellation of Australian queer icons, Courtney is a very bright star indeed; a trailblazer and true interdisciplinarian: all-round performer, author, advocate and globetrotting personality boldly putting Australian creativity on the map. As such, the work was beset with significant material, formal and conceptual challenges.

“My usual choice of material is discarded trash, and my method is collage, yet I was charged with creating a likeness of Courtney, all the while expressing my own artistic point of view in my visual language. The result is a surrealistic junk-art assemblage; a work that exists in a state of flux: halfway between image and sculpture, fantasy and reality, light and dark.”

Courtney Act with her portrait. Photo: National Portrait Gallery.

The portrait is an over life-size mask-like head composed of junk materials, some sourced from his sitter’s dressing room, including leftover sequins, diamantes and acrylic nails. To this, a beer can, a plastic banana, a mobile phone, bits of dolls, a football, shells, sunglasses, stilettos and all sorts of other paraphernalia have been sourced, as well as a tiara-like hair piece that spells out the name ‘Courtney Act’.

It is an engaging piece that will invariably draw a crowd keen to discover the myriad details that went into the work. The scale and glitter may be seen as a celebration of gay culture – like a spectacular Mardi Gras veneer. It may take time to see whether this portrait is seen as a celebration of the artistry and keen intellect we associate with Courtney Act.

The National Portrait Gallery is on King Edward Terrace in front of the High Court and next to the National Gallery of Australia. It’s open every day of the year from 10 am to 5 pm (except 25 December).

canberra.title: Push for review of portable long service leave rejected
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government has rejected a Canberra Liberals proposal for an independent review of the financial impact of expanding portable long...
canberra.content:
Expanded portable long service leave will begin on 1 January 2027, following earlier postponements. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The ACT Government has rejected a Canberra Liberals proposal for an independent review of the financial impact of expanding portable long service leave to hospitality, accommodation, hairdressing and beauty businesses.

The Opposition argues the government must establish whether the scheme could threaten business viability or employment before imposing additional costs on industries already under financial pressure.

But Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister Michael Pettersson told the Legislative Assembly the proposed review would create another obstacle to a reform designed to help workers retain their long service leave entitlements when changing employers.

Under the private member’s bill introduced by Shadow Treasurer Ed Cocks in May this year, the two industries would remain excluded from the expanded scheme until an independent assessment found that their inclusion was unlikely to cause material adverse effects on business viability or employment in the ACT.

The review would have to be conducted by someone who had not worked for the ACT Government, a registered industrial organisation or an employer or employee peak body in the previous five years.

Even with a favourable finding, the expansion could not commence before 1 July 2027. The minister would also have to table the review and reasons for proceeding at least nine Assembly sitting days before making the commencement instrument.

Separate commencement dates could be set for each industry.

The government, however, intends to begin the expansion on 1 January 2027, following earlier postponements.

Portable long service leave allows workers to accumulate qualifying service across different employers in the same industry. Employers contribute to a central fund rather than bearing the full cost of an eligible worker’s leave when it becomes payable.

The standard contribution rate is 1.07 per cent of ordinary wages, with discounted rates being phased in for food and beverage businesses over the first three years.

Liberal MLA James Milligan said cafes, restaurants, community clubs, hairdressers and barbers had raised concerns about additional employment costs.

He argued that hospitality employers were willing to provide long service leave to workers who qualified through continuous service but questioned the suitability of the portable model for their industry.

Milligan also pointed to commercial rates, payroll tax changes and other government charges, arguing that business conditions had not improved since the government previously postponed the expansion.

“If the government is so confident that this policy will help employers and employees, why don’t they want an independent third party review?” he asked.

Canberra Liberal leader Mark Parton cited a Belconnen health and beauty business owner who reportedly said they would no longer employ staff, identifying portable long service leave as a reason.

Mr Pettersson acknowledged the pressures facing businesses but said the government had already delayed commencement and staged the introduction of employer contributions to ease the transition.

He argued that workers in industries characterised by frequent changes of employer could spend decades in their professions without qualifying for long service leave.

“A chef doesn’t stop being a chef because the restaurant they work for closes,” he said.

The minister also questioned whether the Liberals would commit to retaining the expansion if elected in 2028, accusing them of using the review to obstruct a policy they had opposed since its introduction.

The Greens also rejected the bill, arguing that further conditions would leave workers waiting for an entitlement already legislated in 2023.

Greens MLA Andrew Braddock said the expansion had been postponed repeatedly and warned that continued uncertainty could undermine the reform.

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson, however, suggested a middle path: extending support for further scrutiny of the scheme’s levy rates while opposing legislation that would make its commencement conditional on the review’s findings.

“I have to admit the evidence for the levy rate that’s been selected seems pretty thin, so this warrants attention,” he said.

australia.title: Public service union refuses to back Labor at Victorian election, condemning job cuts and $1.2bn consultant spend
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Community and Public Sector Union denounces ‘privatisation by stealth’, joining growing number of unions turning on Carroll go...
australia.content:
Victoria’s public servants union says it will not support Labor at this month’s state election, condemning the government for cutting public service jobs while spending $1.2bn on consultants.

The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) will announce the decision on Wednesday, joining several other unions that have refused to back Labor or are actively campaigning against the government ahead of the 28 November poll.

Although the CPSU’s Victorian branch is not formally affiliated with Labor, it has worked closely with the party in the past. But its secretary, Jiselle Hanna, told Guardian Australia it can no longer support the government.

“If Ben Carroll’s government won’t commit to no job cuts in the public service, then our union cannot support him,” Hanna said.

The Labor government has made successive cuts to the Victorian public service (VPS), a smaller subset of the public sector that is largely administrative, as it seeks to rein in employee expenses – the state’s largest area of expenditure.

This included cutting about 1,000 VPS roles including more than 300 executive positions, and merging several government entities following an independent review, led by Helen Silver, last year. The government has said the changes delivered $4bn in savings, while frontline roles weren’t affected.

As of June 2025, there were some 58,000 employed in the VPS – compared with the almost 400,000 in the total public sector.

Hanna said since the Silver review, there had been more than 200 further restructures, many of which had resulted in “redundancies, job losses and pay cuts”.

“The public service used to be a reliable and secure place to build a career – that job security doesn’t exist any more, it’s been replaced with precarious employment,” she said.

Meanwhile, the Coalition has committed to implementing an indefinite hiring freeze across all back-office public service roles if it wins government, saving $22bn over a decade. The opposition has said the hiring freeze would remain in place until VPS staffing levels returned to the population-adjusted equivalent of 2014–15 – when it was last in government.

Hanna said both Labor and the Coalition’s distinction between frontline public sector roles and back-office VPS roles overlooked work performed by public servants including directing firefighters during bushfires; analysing DNA, fingerprints and ballistics; developing school curricula and investigating childcare centres.

She said while the union accepts “budget savings need to come from somewhere”, cuts to the public service would only lead to increased use of consultants, which she described as “privatisation by stealth”.

Analysis released by the union, based on Victorian government annual reports since the 2017-18 financial year, showed Labor has spent $1.2bn on consultants across 10 departments. The Department of Treasury and Finance had the highest spend of about $222m since 2017, while the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action had the highest annual spend of about $86m in the 2024-25 financial year.

The CPSU has launched a campaign urging Victorians to sign a pledge supporting the public service and committing not to vote for candidates who propose cutting jobs. While the campaign does not endorse any political party, it highlights that both the Greens and the Victorian Socialists oppose public service job cuts and the privatisation of public assets.

Last week, Guardian Australia reported the Electrical Trades Union (ETU) state council resolved not to run a statewide campaign for Labor, despite spending more than $1.6m supporting the party at the last election.

On the same day, the United Firefighters Union – which has been embroiled in a wages dispute with government since 2021 – launched its ad campaign urging Victorians to “put Labor last”.

The Australian Services Union is also running ads calling the premier a liar, as part of its long-term campaign to lift the 1.5% rate cap on councils, which restricts pay rises for workers below inflation.

Members of the Australian Education Union, which is not formally affiliated with the Labor party, have also said they won’t be campaigning for the party. The Health and Community Services Union, meanwhile, has eight members running this election – though none for the Labor party it is affiliated with.

australia.title: I spent 11 years without my childhood friend. Finding our way back together was staggeringly simple
australia.snippet: I thought about her a lot after our friendship imploded. When our birthdays rolled around, I wondered what we’d be doing if we were still...
australia.content:
I was 26 when I lost my childhood friend. By that point, I’d known her for almost two-thirds of my life.

Our first conversation was at an ice-skating party when we were nine years old. I’d been nervous in the weeks leading up to the party because I couldn’t ice-skate. Every time the Spice Girls’ 2 Become 1 music video came on, the sight of Victoria Beckham singing on an ice rink filled me with impending doom. I was sure I would disgrace myself at the party.

But the party – and I don’t often say this about parties – was a blast. As it turned out, my in-line skating experience gave me some advantage on the ice, and I met a girl who was easy to talk to. I was a shy child, so I was struck by that sense of ease – how I wasn’t panicking about what to say or lurking awkwardly on the edge of a conversation. I can’t remember what we talked about. She was kind enough not to mention the fact I’d chosen to wear a dolphin-print sarong. We held hands and at one point she asked: “What’s your name again?” Apparently, we’d had so much to say to each other, we’d skated right over all the usual greetings and pleasantries.

My friend and I went to the same high school, where we developed crushes on Orlando Bloom as Legolas in The Lord of the Rings and became obsessed with Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet when we studied it in our year 9 English class. We loved reading and were into romantasy before it became a global phenomenon. She lent me her box set of Buffy and I made her read my own sexy vampire fan fiction.

As a teenager, I’d always believed I would become myself at university but, when I got there, it was harder and lonelier than I expected. I felt adrift in those first few years and saw less of my friend. We were at different universities, lived further away from each other and life got busy. When I graduated, I started working as a teacher at a large high school and threw myself into the joyous overwhelming chaos of it all.

But then the most exciting thing happened – the stars (and the end of lease agreements) aligned and we decided to get a place together. We moved into a terrace in Sydney’s hip inner west a few days after Christmas. On the first night we sat on the stairs and ate a box of chocolates for dinner. It was like the sleepovers we’d had as children, without supervision. We could do whatever we wanted. And, for a while, we did. We had our friends around. We read on the sunny veranda. We ate and drank our way up and down King Street.

Then one day, I started to feel sick. I thought it might be the iron tablets I was taking, or stress from work. It was diffuse large B cell lymphoma. It knocked me sideways. My prognosis was good from the beginning but the treatment was long, and emotionally I was all over the place.

At 26 I thought that asking for what you wanted was the most embarrassing thing in the world. For that reason, I never put down anything too flashy for my professional learning goals at work. When I went on dates, I aimed to be so casual that I came across as bored, even though I was desperate to be liked. I applied this same winning strategy to cancer. I wanted everyone to think I was fun and cool and not mention the fact that I was sick, and I also wanted their sympathy and for them to acknowledge my suffering. In other words, I wanted them to know instinctively, without being told, what I needed at any given time. It was an impossible demand and I was left disappointed and angry. So I pulled away, which only made me lonely too.

The friendship imploded. She moved out. I made sure I wasn’t around when she picked up her things. I stopped replying to messages and unfollowed her on Facebook. We didn’t speak for 11 years. For a while I was angry and then I was just sad.

I thought about her a lot. When our birthdays rolled around, I considered what we’d be doing if we were still friends. When I met my husband, I wondered what she would think of him. If I read a good novel, I imagined telling her about it. I was desperate to know her take on the Wuthering Heights film.

When you lose a childhood friend, you lose access to a certain part of your life. Without her I had no one to reminisce with about giving our Barbies disturbing makeovers or tearful late-night confessions at sleepovers and long afternoons spent lying on the trampoline, dreaming about our future selves. Back then, our lives were entwined and pulled taut with possibility. I missed her – and I missed that version of myself.

The Instagram algorithm brought us back together this year after more than a decade apart – possibly because we’d been secretly checking in on each other. She followed me and I followed her. She sent me a message, and we met for coffee and cake in the city. It was that staggeringly, heartbreakingly simple.

If I were 26 again (which, thank god, I never will be) I would tell myself that friendship, like all forms of intimacy, requires courage. I wanted my friends to think I was fun and cool and impressive and, when I wasn’t those things, I wanted to hide. It’s frightening to be vulnerable but when you find someone who knows who you are when you stop performing, it’s the greatest relief.

I see my friend regularly now – or as regularly as we can manage given the busyness of work and family. There’s a certain strangeness when one of us mentions a job or partner or trip the other has never heard of, and we are reminded how much of each other’s lives we have missed. But beneath the new strangeness, I sense that old familiar ease.

australia.title: Best TV shows and movies streaming in Australia this month
australia.snippet: Discover what’s coming to Netflix, HBO Max, Disney+, Prime Video and others in October, including an Anthony Bourdain biopic, a new show ...
australia.content:
Netflix

Possible Love

Film, South Korea, 2026 – out 6 November

My colleague Peter Bradshaw is among many critics who have championed this South Korean drama from Lee Chang-dong, which snagged the Silver Lion grand jury prize at this year’s Venice film festival. Inspired by mass layoffs and the subsequent protests that reshaped Korea’s labour movement, the film follows two married couples from opposite ends of the economic spectrum. Lee Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a documentarian, and her husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), are well-off, while Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon) and her husband, Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), a jobless factory worker with a drinking problem, are doing it tough. Ye-ji approaches Mi-ok to feature in her documentary about workers who have lost their jobs.

The film uses the uneven relationship between them to chip away at themes including class division, privilege and exploitation. Bradshaw calls it a “finely judged, beautifully acted” work; “sombre, bittersweet, elegant”.

Allen

Film, Australia, 2026 – out 12 November

Ludo Studio, the Australian production company behind Bluey, pivots to live-action film-making with this family-oriented comedy, which finds a quirky path into a storyline about extraterrestrials and formative experiences. The protagonist is Petey (TJ Power), who’s like a grown-up Elliott from ET the Extra-Terrestrial, and who has never moved on from having an alien pal during childhood (“The best thing that happened to me already happened,” he says). Then one day … guess who returns to say hello?

Its creator and co-director, Daley Pearson, has described Allen as “a story about love, family and all those big and small moments from childhood that end up shaping who we are when we grow up”.

Honourable mentions: The Hobbit 1-3 (film, out now), A Dog’s Perfect Christmas (film, 4 November), Interstellar (film, 5 November), It Ends With Us (film, 6 November, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie (film, 8 November), The Body (TV, 11 November), How the Grinch Stole Christmas (film, 10 November), The Polar Express (film, 12 November), A League of Their Own (film, 13 November), Guiding Stars (film, 18 November), The Altruists (TV, 19 November), Smile (film, 20 November), The Hangover (film, 19 November), Smile (film, 20 November), Steps (film, 20 November), The Mosquito Bowl (film, 25 November), Sonic the Hedgehog (film, 27 November), Michael (film, 29 November).

Stan

Storm Bird

Film, Australia, 2026 – out 4 November

From the outset, the beats of this Australian indie are soft and contemplative, making the most of a small cast and modest settings. The protagonist is Jack (James Ivor), a construction worker soon to go to prison. His neighbour is Richard (Anthony Phelan), a well-known cellist whom Jack comes to the aid of when he suffers a heart attack. The pair don’t get along but this event profoundly changes their relationship, which deepens during the days leading up to Jack’s stint in the slammer.

It doesn’t take long to feel as though you’re in good hands, with co-directors James Ivor and Eryk Lenartowicz chipping away at their characters patiently and thoughtfully. The drama has a pleasingly unhurried quality, ultimately feeling a tad open-ended – remaining sincere and quietly affecting throughout.

The Death of Robin Hood

Film, USA, 2026 – out 13 November

The latest Robin Hood adventure sure ain’t Men in Tights. The modus operandi embraced by the writer/director Michael Sarnoski seems to have been: “Let’s take the story of that dude who stole from the rich to give to the poor, and make it unrelentingly dark and morose.” Billed with the poster tagline “He was no hero,” Hugh Jackman – sporting his most prodigiously bushy beard yet – plays the eponymous character, who, in this version of the story, is a violent scumbag who has murdered many people, including children.

Yeah … it’s dark. As I wrote earlier this year, it “feels like we’re being asked to emotionally invest in a character who is irredeemably awful”. Aesthetically, though, the film “has ugly bravado, with a savage, burnt-out, bleached kind of beauty”.

Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret

Film, USA, 2023 – out 22 November

Kelly Fremon Craig’s adaptation of Judy Blume’s classic coming-of-age novel is delightfully staged, with top-notch writing and direction. Abby Ryder Fortson delivers a wonderful leading performance as the eponymous Margaret, who’s desperate to grow up, grow breasts and get her period. As an adult, you feel like saying, “Slow down and enjoy your youth – it’ll be gone soon.”

  • Sign up for the fun stuff with our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morning

The film is interspersed with memorable voiceover narration in the form of prayers to the big dude upstairs, though the tone is indeed more “are you there?” than religious reverence, with the protagonist ultimately describing herself as an atheist.

Honourable mentions: Unskilled Adult (TV, out now), The Notebook (film, out now), Mr Deeds (film, 10 November), The Good Daughter (TV, 13 November), Smile (film, 20 November), Big Daddy (film, 24 November), The Craft (film, 26 November), Another Simple Favour (film, 27 November), Gnomeo & Juliet (film, 27 November), The Departed (film, 28 November), Blade Runner 2049 (film, 28 November).

SBS on Demand

Tangerine

Film, USA, 2015 – out 13 November

My favourite Christmas movie of all time is Sean Baker’s micro-budget, iPhone-shot comedy-drama about transgender sex workers in Los Angeles. It comes on like a clap of thunder, with a frenetic pace and hyper-stylised aesthetic, while maintaining an airtight sense of verisimilitude. “Merry Christmas Eve, bitch!” is the opening line, delivered by Sin-Dee Rella (Kitana Kiki Rodriguez), who has just been released from prison and is catching up with her best friend, Alexandra (Mya Taylor), in a doughnut shop.

When Sin-Dee hears that her beau has been cheating on her “with some white fish”, she tears through the city like a wrecking ball, hunting down the woman. When I spoke to Baker – who subsequently directed the best picture winner Anora – he told me that Tangerine was originally conceived in a social-realist style. But he “pumped saturation through the roof” because “these women’s personalities were just so colourful”.

Russian Ark

Film, Russia, 2002 – out 20 November

It might sound like a tired turn of phrase but there really is nothing like Alexander Sokurov’s majestically staged single-shot film, which turns St Petersburg’s Hermitage Museum into a time machine, capturing the space splendidly while drifting dream-like across three centuries of Russian history. The camera glides around like a dancer, and, in fact, dances along with the human performers, in an extraordinary ballroom sequence late in the runtime, depicting a 1913 ball held to celebrate the 300th anniversary of the Romanov dynasty. Russian Ark is a dazzling mixture of opulence, beauty and cinematic daring.

Honourable mentions: Grand Torino (film, out now), City on a Hill seasons 1-3 (TV, out now), Deli Boys (TV, 5 November), The Sapphires (film, 6 November), Ghost in the Shell 2: Innocence (film, 6 November), 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback (TV, 10 November), Practical Magic (film, 13 November), Boiling Point (film, 13 November), Cardinal seasons 1-4 (TV, 19 November), A Hard Day’s Night (film, 20 November), Universal Soldier (film, 20 November), Dying for Sex (TV, 26 November).

HBO Max

Goodfellas

Film, USA, 1990 – out 7 November

Certain things in life go together brilliantly – like horses and carts, wine and cheese, and Martin Scorsese and gangster movies. Goodfellas follows Ray Liotta’s protagonist Henry Hill, who opens the film with that immortal declaration: “As far back as I can remember, I always wanted to be a gangster.” And he certainly gets his gangster game on, climbing the criminal ranks and fraternising with some rather iffy company, including his mentor, Jimmy (Robert De Niro), and the frighteningly volatile Tommy (Joe Pesci, bringing the house down with his signature brand of combustible menace).

The story springs to life like a frog in a sock and the staging is superb. Scorsese deploys audacious directorial flourishes, including the iconic Copacabana tracking shot – a single take that follows Henry and his wife, Karen (Lorraine Bracco, who later played Tony Soprano’s psychiatrist in The Sopranos), through a nightclub’s back corridors and into its dining room.

George Carlin’s American Dream

TV, USA, 2022 – out 20 November

There’s no doubt that George Carlin ranks among the all-time greatest US comedians, though he was perhaps more like a mad prophet of the airways than a joke-maker. Judd Apatow and Michael Bonfiglio’s two-part documentary about his life is fairly conventional in structure, mixing talking heads with archival footage and, naturally, plenty of choice bits from Carlin’s standup routines. But as they say, conventions are conventions for a reason: the film hangs together nicely, with a brisk pace and interesting insights.

Honourable mentions: Adultery (TV, out now), Hunting Season (film, 6 November), The Many Saints of Newark (film, 7 November) Deep Water (film, 13 November), City of God: The Fight Rages On season 2 (TV, 8 November), 4 Blocks Zero (TV, 13 November), Inherent Vice (film, 14 November), When a Witness Recants (film, 18 November), I, Object (film, 20 November), The Slightest Touch (film, 26 November).

Prime Video

Tony

Film, USA, 2026 – out now

Matt Johnson wisely went into his Anthony Bourdain biopic thinking that any film about the late author, presenter and food critic should have a whole lotta sass. Set in 1975, when Bourdain was a 19-year-old student working in a seafood restaurant, the story has coming-of-age-esque vibes – early love, bad decisions, hot emotions. But it’s the central character – played by Dominic Sessa with an appealing blend of charm and prickliness – that really makes it pop. The film is tightly directed by Johnson, who also helmed the clever and charming tech origins drama BlackBerry.

Blade Runner 2099

TV, USA, 2026 – out 25 November

Great-looking cyberpunk productions have a complex kind of beauty, marrying eye-watering compositions with a feeling that something has gone terribly wrong. The two Blade Runner movies are brilliant examples of this and the trailer for the franchise’s first television series suggests it may match them visually.

Narrative-wise, we’ll have to wait and see; we do know that replicants are now the most powerful beings on Earth, supplanting smelly old humans. Michelle Yeoh plays Olwen, a replicant whose time is nearly up and whose story will presumably serve as a launchpad – as Rick Deckard’s did in the original movie and K’s in the sequel – to explore meaty themes surrounding consciousness, mortality and that oldie but a goodie: what makes us human?

Honourable mentions: Now You See Me 1 and 2 (film, out now), Desperate Housewives seasons 1-8 (TV, out now), Sing 2 (film, out now), The Chronicles of Narnia: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader (film, out now), The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (film, out now), The Greatest (TV, 4 November), The Mongoose (film, 4 November), The Lord of The Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 (TV, 11 November), Twilight 1-5 (film, 18 November), Hokum (film, 26 November).

Disney+

Rivals – season 2, part 2

TV, UK, 2026 – 11 November

If you’ve never seen this racy period comedy set in the British TV industry during the 80s, it’s certainly worth a watch, with its sly humour, chaotic pace and outrageously colourful characters. The title refers to the ongoing war between David Tennant’s media mogul, Tony Baddingham, and Alex Hassell’s sex-obsessed aristocrat, Rupert Campbell-Black, their feud turning the industry into a war zone. “Revenge is a dish best served on television,” Tennant says early in the first season, that whiff of delicious menace in his voice reflecting the show’s gleefully wicked spirit, delivered with a knowing wink.

Honourable mentions: Meet the Parents (film, 1 November), Meet the Fockers (film, 1 November), Tropic Thunder (film, 1 November), A Quiet Place (film, 1 November), Dr Seuss’ How the Grinch Stole Christmas (film, 1 November), The Grinch (film, 1 November), All’s Fair season 2 (TV, 4 November), Time and Water (film, 5 November), The Polar Express (film, 15 November), Percy Jackson and the Olympians (TV, 20 November).

Binge

Dig

TV, USA, 2026 – out 23 November

Mike Schur has form when it comes to launching quality comedy series, having created The Good Place and co-created Brooklyn Nine-Nine and Parks and Recreation. Amy Poehler, star of the latter, reunites with Schur for this workplace comedy set in the world of archaeology. She plays Elise, an ambitious archaeologist chomping at the bit for a promotion. So when she makes a major discovery at an excavation site in Greece, temptation beckons: why not keep it under wraps for now, so she can claim all the credit later?

The trailer suggests a more narrative-driven affair than Parks and Recreation. If it’s even half as funny, it’ll be worth a watch.

Honourable mentions: Michael Jackson’s This Is It (film, out now), It’s Never Over, Jeff Buckley (film, out now), The Super Mario Galaxy Movie (film, 8 November), JFK: 24 Hours That Changed the World (film, 22 November), Catch Me If You Can season 1 (TV, 26 November).

AppleTV+

12 12 12

TV, USA, 2026 – out 13 November

The title of this heist drama starring Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan refers to the three timelines the series oscillates between as it chronicles an elaborate bank robbery in Zurich. There are the 12 months it took to plan, the 12 hours it took to execute and the 12 days immediately after it. But why stop there? What about 12 seconds when the characters think: “Shit, can we really do this?” Or the previous 12 centuries, charting the evolution of Switzerland and the development of its banking system?

Anyway … the trailer certainly promises juicy spectacle, with overturned vehicles, explosions, sex and puffed-up dialogue like: “Only one of us should get to walk away from this thing.”

Honourable mentions: Stick season 2 (TV, 4 November), Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook (TV, 6 November), Being Heumann (film, 13 November), Way of the Warrior Kid (film, 25 November).

australia.title: For Avelima’s family, every RBA rate hike means more shifts, a stretched budget – and less time together
australia.snippet: Australian families feel like the goalposts are ‘constantly moving’ as they face the impact of a fifth rate rise Get our breaking news em...
australia.content:
Sydney mum Avelima Satiu and her husband, Chris, each work two jobs to keep their household afloat. For the couple, every interest rate rise means more shifts, less time together and a family budget stretched even thinner.

“We have to review our budget; we usually look at how many extra shifts we can pick up,” Satiu says. “Even if it’s like an extra $100 or $200 that we get a month, that usually is enough to cover that rate hike.”

The Satius are among millions of mortgage holders left reeling from the Reserve Bank of Australia’s decision to lift its key interest rate on Tuesday from 4.6% to 4.85%, the highest since 2008.

The family lives in a four-bedroom home in the south-western Sydney suburb of Gregory Hills. With a mortgage of about $850,000, they pay about $1,350 a week in repayments.

Satiu, 36, works a nine-to-five job in finance and does freelance social media work on the side. Her husband works full-time in insurance and does disability support work on weekends. They work between 50 and 60 hours a week each.

“We don’t get to spend as much time as a family as we would like. A lot of the time is spent away from my kids. My husband works every weekend, he works seven days a week and his hours are long … but it’s the sacrifice we’re willing to make,” she says.

The couple’s youngest child arrived five months ago, and Satiu is back at work. They save thousands of dollars on childcare by “leaning on our village” and having an aunt live with them to care for the children while the couple works.

For Satiu, a second-generation Samoan who grew up below the poverty line and spent much of her childhood in public housing, it can feel like “the goalposts are constantly moving”.

“My parents were constantly struggling, and it was so stressful and it was such a negative environment. I feel like when you’re so excited because you get to own the home you’re in, then there are all these bills and then on top of that, your mortgage continually moves … It’s very hard to get ahead.”

After five consecutive rate hikes, Satiu says the blows are starting to feel “inevitable” and “the only thing that [I] can do is make sure that we’re ready for it”.

‘There has to be a different way’

Tiffany Betts is a 37-year-old university staff member who lives in Nowra, on the south coast of New South Wales, with her 67-year-old mother. In 2021, the pair pooled their savings to buy a house after decades of poor renting experiences.

Her mother, a former school teacher who is now fully retired, provided most of the deposit, while Betts pays the monthly mortgage repayments of about $1,200 a fortnight.

She says she feels her life has been stripped back to the bare minimum, constantly “scratching around” to find cuts to her budget to make ends meet.

“It’s tight, and it’s pretty confronting and nerve-racking. I am very frugal with my money. I don’t eat out, we very rarely go to the movies or spend on extras. There’s not really room for non-essential bits and pieces,” she says.

She says she feels the Australian dream “just doesn’t ring true any more” and that she is “stuck on a hamster wheel”.

“I work hard, I earn good money, and I still can’t get ahead in life. I live paycheque to paycheque because there’s just not the money left over to put into savings.”

Speaking after the announcement, the RBA governor, Michele Bullock, said that “this is not the news that many Australians want to hear, but it is what’s needed to get inflation down”.

“Every household is dealing with higher prices for groceries, electricity, insurance and other essentials. High inflation is particularly painful for Australians on lower incomes, including people who rent and have little or no savings to fall back on when most of your income is already going towards essentials; there is nowhere left to cut spending,” Bullock said.

“Some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track.”

Betts says this week’s rate hike only adds to her “frustration and anger” as a homeowner.

“Homeowners are feeling the brunt of this, and we should not be having to do the heavy lifting for the whole economy. There has to be a better way, and other ways to share this burden more equitably across society,” she says.

“There has to be a different way to leave interest rates alone but still get the same impact of taking money out of the economy, one that shares it across the majority of society.”

australia.title: Snowy Hydro 2.0 executives awarded bonuses totalling $751,925 despite cost blowout
australia.snippet: Annual reports show NSW renewable company’s CEO opted out of cash bonus, while CSIRO’s chief received an extra $200,000 Get our breaking ...
australia.content:
Executives at the troubled Snowy Hydro company collectively banked bonuses worth a combined $751,925 in the last financial year, despite its renewable energy project blowing out to 12 times its original cost.

But Guardian Australia can reveal chief executive, Dennis Barnes, who has a base salary of $1,845,126, opted not to accept the extra cash.

The company’s chief financial officer, Kim Josling, who has a pay packet worth $828,839, received a $215,440 bonus, according to the company’s annual report for the 2025-2026 financial year.

Its chief operating officer, Maia Schweizer, received a base salary of $1,050,503, and pocketed a $255,570 bonus, while chief commercial officer, Gordon Wymer, who has a base salary of $1,142,268, took home a $280,915 bonus.

The company’s long-delayed renewable energy project, Snowy Hydro 2.0, will not be completed until the end of the decade and is expected to cost taxpayers as much as $25bn.

It was first put forward in 2017 by the Turnbull government and came with an original price tag of $2bn, but the project in the Kosciuszko national park has climbed in cost.

The project was revised to almost $13bn in 2023, and construction was expected to completed by the end of 2028.

Snowy 2.0 now won’t be completed and fully commissioned until 2029.

A Snowy Hydro spokesperson said “short term incentives are based on a range of performance outcomes across these parts of Snowy Hydro’s business”.

“Mr Barnes recommended to Snowy Hydro’s Board that he receive no short term incentive payment for FY26,” the statement reads.

At Australia’s national science agency, the CSIRO, its chief executive, Doug Hilton, received a bonus of $198,517 on top of his $789,391 base salary, according to its 2025-2026 annual report.

He was the only one of the organisation’s senior executives to receive a bonus classed as a “salary at risk” payment.

The cash was awarded the same year the agency made a number of painful cuts, shrinking its workforce by several hundred people.

More than 1,100 jobs have been cut from CSIRO in the last two years, according to the Community and Public Sector Union.

Separation and redundancy payments cost the agency more than $27m.

A CSIRO spokesperson said the agency’s board determined the annual value of the “at risk payment” which was assessed on key performance indicators.

Bonus payments to other senior executives were removed in the 2021-2022 financial year to align the agency with the public service, where such payments were also being removed.

“The size of CSIRO’s workforce is now expected to remain stable, supported by additional funding from the Australian Government in this year’s federal budget,” the spokesperson said.

“CSIRO acknowledges that change can create uncertainty for affected staff, and we do not underestimate the impact of that.”

world.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
world.snippet: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering ill...
world.content:
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.

South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.

Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.

The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.

However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.

“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.

“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

world.title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
world.snippet: Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF Members of the Sudanese ...
world.content:
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.

Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.

There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”

He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.

“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”

Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

world.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
world.snippet: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah,...
world.content:
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.

Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

world.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
world.snippet: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and pos...
world.content:
The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.

“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.

On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.

The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.

Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.

The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.

Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.

“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.

At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”

Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.

“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

world.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
world.snippet: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected t...
world.content:
Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.

A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.

The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.

The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.

Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.

A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”

During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.

The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.
